sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** HTTPS is HTTP layered over TLS (Transport Layer Security), providing confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for web traffic by encrypting the HTTP request and response with keys negotiated through a handshake that authenticates the server (and optionally the client) using X.509 certificates.
HTTPS is what makes the modern web trustworthy. Without TLS, every HTTP request travels in cleartext over TCP, meaning any router, ISP, coffee-shop Wi-Fi, or compromised switch along the path can read your passwords, modify the response, or impersonate the server. TLS solves three problems at once: confidentiality (encryption prevents eavesdropping), integrity (MAC/AEAD prevents tampering), and authentication (the server proves its identity via a certificate chain rooted in a trusted CA). The TLS 1.2 handshake takes 2 RTTs: ClientHello → ServerHello+Certificate+ServerKeyExchange+ServerHelloDone → ClientKeyExchange+ChangeCipherSpec+Finished → ChangeCipherSpec+Finished. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, 2018) collapsed this to 1 RTT by combining key exchange into the ClientHello/ServerHello using ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, and added 0-RTT mode for resumed sessions that lets the client send encrypted data on the very first flight. This 1-RTT reduction is significant on mobile networks: at 200 ms RTT, it saves 200 ms per cold connection, which is why Google, Cloudflare, and Facebook pushed hard for adoption.

The TLS handshake is conceptually a four-step dance. (1) The client sends ClientHello listing supported cipher suites, TLS versions, and a random number; (2) the server picks a cipher suite and version, sends its certificate (which contains its public key signed by a CA), and a ServerHello random; (3) the two sides perform a key exchange — in TLS 1.3 this is ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, where each side raises the other's public DH value to their own private exponent to derive a shared secret that an eavesdropper cannot compute; (4) both sides switch to encrypted mode and exchange Finished messages that authenticate the entire handshake transcript, preventing man-in-the-middle tampering. After the handshake, application data flows encrypted using an AEAD cipher like AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, which provides both confidentiality and integrity in a single operation. Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) means that even if the server's long-term private key is leaked in the future, past captured traffic cannot be decrypted — because the per-session keys were derived from ephemeral DH values that were never stored and are now gone.

Why does this matter in real systems? Because HTTPS is now mandatory for almost everything — browsers flag HTTP as "not secure," HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 require TLS in practice (even though the spec allows cleartext), and app stores reject apps that send sensitive data over HTTP. Real-world: Cloudflare was one of the earliest large-scale TLS 1.3 deployers and pioneered 0-RTT optimization, which lets returning clients send data on the first flight — they reported saving an average of ~150 ms per connection. Google enforces HTTPS everywhere internally and externally: Gmail, Search, and Drive all use TLS 1.3 with PFS by default, and Chrome marks HTTP sites as insecure, which pushed the entire web to migrate (the percentage of HTTPS web traffic rose from ~30% in 2015 to ~85% in 2024 per W3Techs). Amazon enforced HTTPS for all AWS API calls and offers free certificates via AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to remove the cost barrier. Let's Encrypt, launched in 2015, made TLS certificates free and automatic, which is the single biggest reason the long tail of websites adopted HTTPS.

The certificate chain is the trust anchor. A server's leaf certificate is signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root CA (e.g., DigiCert, Let's Encrypt's ISRG Root X1). The root CAs are pre-installed in your OS or browser's trust store. When the client receives the server's cert chain, it verifies each signature up to a trusted root, checks that the cert's domain matches the requested hostname (SAN/CN), checks the validity dates, and revokes via OCSP or CRL. If any check fails, the browser shows a scary warning. A common pitfall is certificate mismanagement: forgetting to renew (Let's Encrypt certs expire every 90 days), missing SAN for `www` vs apex, or serving the wrong cert from a load balancer. Another pitfall is HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), a header (`Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload`) that tells the browser "always use HTTPS for this domain for the next year, and never accept a downgrade to HTTP." Once set, it cannot be undone quickly — if you set HSTS and then need to revert to HTTP for some reason, browsers will refuse for the duration of max-age. The `preload` directive opts the domain into browser HSTS lists, which is even harder to reverse.

The trade-off: TLS adds CPU cost (asymmetric crypto for the handshake, symmetric crypto for data), latency (1 RTT for TLS 1.3, 2 RTT for TLS 1.2), and operational complexity (cert management, rotation, revocation). Modern Intel/AMD CPUs have AES-NI and AVX-512 instructions that make symmetric crypto essentially free (10+ Gbps per core), and ECDSA and ECDHE are fast enough that handshake cost is dominated by RTT, not CPU. Cloud providers offload TLS to load balancers (AWS ALB/NLB, Cloudflare's edge) so application servers see cleartext. The other trade-off is inspection: TLS breaks deep packet inspection (DPI), which is why corporate firewalls and antivirus tools sometimes MITM TLS with a locally-installed CA — a practice that breaks end-to-end security and is increasingly controversial.

HTTPS connects to every networking concept: it sits on top of TCP (Topic 2) and wraps HTTP (Topic 3), enables HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and is the substrate for secure cookies, OAuth tokens, and mTLS service-to-service auth in microservices (Phase 8). It also connects to Phase 1's reliability topic — a TLS handshake failure is a 100% availability failure for the affected clients. Latency budgets (Phase 1, Topic 8) must include TLS handshake RTT, and performance-conscious teams measure "time to first byte" with and without TLS to understand the cost.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    participant CA as Certificate Authority

    Note over C,CA: Pre-condition: CA root is in client trust store

    Note over C,S: TLS 1.3 handshake (1 RTT)
    C->>S: ClientHello (cipher suites, versions, key_share, SNI)
    S->>CA: (offline) CA signed server's leaf cert earlier
    S->>C: ServerHello (chosen cipher, key_share) + EncryptedExtensions + Certificate + CertVerify + Finished
    Note over C: verify cert chain -> trusted root, check hostname, check dates
    Note over C: derive shared secret via ECDHE (client_priv * server_pub)
    C->>S: Finished (encrypts handshake transcript)
    Note over C,S: Application data flows encrypted (AEAD)

    Note over C,S: TLS 1.3 0-RTT (resumed session)
    C->>S: ClientHello + early_data (already encrypted with PSK)
    S->>C: ServerHello + ... (accepts or rejects 0-RTT)
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
TLS 1.2 handshake (2 RTT before app data):
  RTT1:  C --ClientHello-->               S
         C <--ServerHello+Cert+ServerKeyExchange+ServerHelloDone-- S
  RTT2:  C --ClientKeyExchange+ChangeCipherSpec+Finished-->       S
         C <--ChangeCipherSpec+Finished--                         S
  RTT3:  C --(encrypted app data)-->                              S

TLS 1.3 handshake (1 RTT before app data):
  RTT1:  C --ClientHello(+key_share+SNI)-->                       S
         C <--ServerHello(+key_share)+Cert+CertVerify+Finished--  S
         C --Finished-->                                          S  (can carry app data)
  RTT2+: C --(encrypted app data)-->                              S

TLS 1.3 0-RTT (returning client with PSK from prior session):
  RTT0:  C --ClientHello+early_data(encrypted with PSK)-->        S
         (server may accept or reject 0-RTT, then proceeds with 1-RTT handshake)

Certificate chain verification:
+----------------+
| Root CA (ISRG) |  <-- pre-installed in OS/browser trust store
+----------------+
        | signs
+----------------+
| Intermediate   |  <-- sent in server's cert chain
+----------------+
        | signs
+----------------+
| Leaf (example) |  <-- server's actual cert (matches SNI)
+----------------+

Cipher suite components (TLS 1.3):
  TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
  |     |             |-> HMAC / hash for handshake transcript
  |     |-> AEAD symmetric cipher for data (AES-GCM)
  |-> key exchange / authentication (ECDHE + ECDSA, fixed in 1.3)
```

### Walkthrough
1. The client sends ClientHello listing supported ciphers and TLS versions, plus a Diffie-Hellman public key share and the SNI (Server Name Indication) so the server knows which cert to serve.
2. The server replies with ServerHello (chosen cipher, its own DH share), its certificate (signed by a CA), a signature over the handshake transcript (CertVerify), and a Finished message. The client verifies the cert chain up to a trusted root, checks the hostname and dates, derives the shared secret via ECDHE, and sends its own Finished.
3. From this point, application data flows encrypted with AEAD. In TLS 1.3 0-RTT, a returning client uses a pre-shared key from a prior session to encrypt early data on the very first flight — saving a full RTT at the cost of weaker replay protection.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- TLS 1.3 handshake state machine (mock).
- In TLS 1.3, the server also sends Certificate, CertVerify, Finished
- In the same flight; we add them as separate messages for clarity.
- Verify the cert chain reaches a trusted root.
- Verify the hostname matches the leaf cert's SAN.
- Derive shared secret (placeholder; real TLS uses ECDHE).

**Defines:** `State`, `HandshakeMessage`, `TLSConnection`, `run_handshake()`

```python
"""
TLS 1.3 handshake state machine (mock).

This is NOT real cryptography -- it models the state transitions of the TLS
handshake so you can see the sequence of messages and verify each side ends
up in the "Connected" state. Real TLS uses ECDHE for key exchange and AEAD
for data encryption; we use placeholder bytes here.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum, auto
from typing import Optional

class State(Enum):
    START = auto()
    CLIENT_HELLO_SENT = auto()
    SERVER_HELLO_SENT = auto()
    CLIENT_FINISHED_SENT = auto()
    CONNECTED = auto()
    CLOSED = auto()

@dataclass
class HandshakeMessage:
    name: str
    payload: dict

@dataclass
class TLSConnection:
    role: str                      # "client" or "server"
    state: State = State.START
    sent: list = field(default_factory=list)
    received: list = field(default_factory=list)
    shared_secret: Optional[bytes] = None
    cert_chain: list = field(default_factory=list)
    cipher_suite: Optional[str] = None

    # ---- Client side ----
    def send_client_hello(self) -> HandshakeMessage:
        assert self.role == "client" and self.state == State.START
        msg = HandshakeMessage("ClientHello", {
            "versions": ["tls1.3"],
            "cipher_suites": ["TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256", "TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256"],
            "key_share": b"client_dh_pub_placeholder",
            "sni": "example.com",
            "random": b"client_random_xxxxxx",
        })
        self.sent.append(msg)
        self.state = State.CLIENT_HELLO_SENT
        return msg

    # ---- Server side ----
    def handle_client_hello(self, msg: HandshakeMessage,
                            cert_chain: list) -> HandshakeMessage:
        assert self.role == "server" and self.state == State.START
        self.received.append(msg)
        self.cipher_suite = "TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256"
        self.cert_chain = cert_chain
        reply = HandshakeMessage("ServerHello", {
            "version": "tls1.3",
            "cipher_suite": self.cipher_suite,
            "key_share": b"server_dh_pub_placeholder",
            "random": b"server_random_yyyyyy",
        })
        self.sent.append(reply)
        # In TLS 1.3, the server also sends Certificate, CertVerify, Finished
        # in the same flight; we add them as separate messages for clarity.
        self.sent.append(HandshakeMessage("Certificate", {"chain": cert_chain}))
        self.sent.append(HandshakeMessage("CertVerify", {"sig": b"sig_over_transcript"}))
        self.sent.append(HandshakeMessage("Finished", {"verify_data": b"server_finished_mac"}))
        self.state = State.SERVER_HELLO_SENT
        return reply

    # ---- Client side ----
    def handle_server_flight(self, messages: list, trust_roots: set) -> None:
        assert self.role == "client" and self.state == State.CLIENT_HELLO_SENT
        self.received.extend(messages)
        # Verify the cert chain reaches a trusted root.
        cert_msg = next(m for m in messages if m.name == "Certificate")
        chain = cert_msg.payload["chain"]
        if chain[-1] not in trust_roots:
            raise ValueError("cert chain does not reach a trusted root")
        # Verify the hostname matches the leaf cert's SAN.
        leaf = chain[0]
        if "example.com" not in leaf:
            raise ValueError("hostname mismatch")
        # Derive shared secret (placeholder; real TLS uses ECDHE).
        self.shared_secret = b"derived_shared_secret_zzz"
        # Send Finished.
        fin = HandshakeMessage("Finished", {"verify_data": b"client_finished_mac"})
        self.sent.append(fin)
        self.state = State.CLIENT_FINISHED_SENT

    # ---- Server side ----
    def handle_client_finished(self, msg: HandshakeMessage) -> None:
        assert self.role == "server" and self.state == State.SERVER_HELLO_SENT
        self.received.append(msg)
        self.shared_secret = b"derived_shared_secret_zzz"
        self.state = State.CONNECTED

    def finalize(self) -> None:
        if self.role == "client":
            assert self.state == State.CLIENT_FINISHED_SENT
        self.state = State.CONNECTED

    def send_app_data(self, data: bytes) -> None:
        assert self.state == State.CONNECTED, "must finish handshake first"
        print(f"  [{self.role}] sending {len(data)}B encrypted app data")

def run_handshake():
    client = TLSConnection(role="client")
    server = TLSConnection(role="server")

    print("=== TLS 1.3 handshake simulation ===")
    ch = client.send_client_hello()
    print(f"1. client -> server : {ch.name}")

    sh = server.handle_client_hello(ch, cert_chain=["leaf_example.com", "intermediate", "ISRG_Root_X1"])
    print(f"2. server -> client : ServerHello + Certificate + CertVerify + Finished")

    trust_roots = {"ISRG_Root_X1"}
    server_flight = [m for m in server.sent if m.name in
                     ("ServerHello", "Certificate", "CertVerify", "Finished")]
    client.handle_server_flight(server_flight, trust_roots)
    print(f"3. client -> server : Finished (cert chain verified, secret derived)")

    server.handle_client_finished(client.sent[-1])
    print(f"4. server : secret derived, state -> CONNECTED")

    client.finalize()
    print(f"\nclient state: {client.state.name}")
    print(f"server state: {server.state.name}")
    print(f"shared secret matches: {client.shared_secret == server.shared_secret}")

    print("\n=== Application data over encrypted channel ===")
    client.send_app_data(b"GET /secret HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\n\r\n")
    server.send_app_data(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 5\r\n\r\nhello")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_handshake()
```

quiz.question: What problem does TLS solve that plain HTTP does not?
options: Certificate revocation is the broken part of the TLS ecosystem.
TLS 1.3 is not supported by very old clients (Android 4.x, old IE, some embedded devices), and TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated (RFC 8996) and disabled by modern browsers.
Immediate fix: identify which certs expired (check the LB, the CDN, and any internal services), then renew via your CA (Let's Encrypt, ACM, DigiCert).
TLS solves three problems: confidentiality, integrity, and authentication.
quiz.explanation: TLS solves three problems: confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. Confidentiality: the HTTP request and response are encrypted with symmetric keys derived during the handshake, so an eavesdropper on the wire sees only ciphertext. Integrity: every TLS record carries a MAC or AEAD tag that detects tampering — if a man-in-the-middle modifies a byte, the tag won't verify and the connection is torn down.

quiz.explanation: Perfect Forward Secrecy means that even if the server's long-term private key is leaked in the future, past captured traffic cannot be decrypted. This is achieved by using ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) for key exchange: each session derives its keys from random per-session DH values that are never stored and are erased when the connection closes.

A server presents a chain: leaf cert (for example.com) → intermediate CA cert → root CA cert.
quiz.explanation: A server presents a chain: leaf cert (for example.com) → intermediate CA cert → root CA cert. The root CA's public key is pre-installed in the client's OS or browser trust store (e.g., ISRG Root X1 for Let's Encrypt, DigiCert, GlobalSign). The client verifies each signature: the leaf is signed by the intermediate, the intermediate is signed by the root.
